html:
The siege of Orléans lasted from 12 October 1428 to 8 May 1429 at Orléans on the Loire, in central France. A French army inspired by Joan of Arc drove off the English, and the Hundred Years' War turned.

After Agincourt, the English and their ally Burgundy held Paris and the north of France. The French heir, the Dauphin Charles, held the land south of the Loire but had not been crowned. Orléans guarded the main crossing of the river. The English had too few men to surround the city, so they built forts around it and waited. By spring the defenders were close to giving up. Then Joan, a peasant girl of about seventeen who said God had sent her, convinced Charles to let her ride with a relief force. She entered the city on 29 April. Within days she led attacks that took the main English forts. The English marched away.

The French won again at Patay in June, and in July the Dauphin was crowned at Reims as Charles VII. England never recovered the advantage, and by 1453 it had lost everything but Calais.
